title: Off Broadway Review: THE RECEPTIONIST - Bored and Confused?

Well, I knew it was written by Adam Bock. I'm not super familiar with his work, but I do know his name and I am familiar with some of what he's done. I also knew it starred Kate Finneran, who I am a big fan of. She is very funny, very talented, and I have loved her in everything I've ever seen her in. Other than that, I was going in pretty fresh, except I also knew it was written about 20 years ago and that this is a revival. So, before I go on, let me tell you that this is an excellent production of a fascinating play and it will be impossible to talk about it without giving away some surprises. Thanks, I really appreciate it. So, let me give you a little background on this play. Adam Bock is a Canadian-American playwright who has been a significant voice in Off-Broadway theater for decades. He is known for works like Swimming in the Shallows, The Drunken City, and The Thugs, for which he won an Obie Award. He also received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2012. His writing tends to blend quirky, almost whimsical comedic surfaces with genuinely dark and unsettling undercurrents. He is, in the best possible way, a playwright who makes you laugh right up until he makes you deeply uncomfortable. Now, The Receptionist was developed with support from the Eugene O'Neill Center at the National Playwrights Conference in 2006. And had a staged reading at Hartford Stage's brand new festival around the same time. It then received its world premiere in October 2007 at the Manhattan Theatre Club directed by the Tony Award-winning Joe Mantello and starring Jane Houdyshell as Beverly. Gosh, I wish I'd seen that production. Mantello is one of the best directors working and Houdyshell is so perfect for this role. Not surprisingly, that production sold out and was extended. Critically, the play was embraced. The New York Times called it a quote poisoned post-it note of a play and critics praised its ability to make the mundane deeply unsettling. It was nominated for outstanding off-Broadway play at the Outer Critics Circle Awards and included in the best plays of 2007-2008 anthology. The play was written in the final years of the Bush administration as questions about government-sanctioned torture and institutional complicity were very much part of the national conversation. That context is baked right into the DNA of this piece and it turns out the DNA hasn't aged a day, unfortunately. So, what is The Receptionist about? On its surface, it's a comedy about office life. Beverly, played here by Kate Finneran, is the receptionist at a company whose true nature is slowly revealed to us over the course of the play. She works alongside her colleague Lorraine, played by Mallory Johnson, and their boss Edward Raymond, played by Nia Nacer. Things shift when a man named Martin Dart, played by Will Pullen, arrives from the central office and it becomes clear pretty quickly that he is not there for a routine visit. The play is one-act, clocking in at about 80 minutes with no intermission, and there are just four characters. Part of what makes it work is that Bach doesn't hand you exposition on a silver platter. You piece together what this company actually does as you watch. It seems to be set somewhere around the early 2000s. There are references to laptops and the internet, but Beverly is using a Rolodex and faxes are going off in the background. So, it has this transitional era quality that suits the story well. Let me start with the positives because there are a lot of them. First and foremost, the acting. This is an outstanding cast. Kate Finneran is doing exactly what you'd hope she'd do. She is funny, she is warm, she has impeccable timing, and she makes Beverly completely real. Beverly is a woman with very strong opinions about other people's love lives. And her phone conversations with friends throughout the play are hilarious. Mallory Johnson as Lorraine is a wonderful foil and scene partner, and together Finneran and Johnson have a great chemistry. And their dynamic, Beverly the receptionist, Lorraine a rung above her on the office ladder, is the beating heart of the show. Will Pullen and Nima Nassar round out the cast beautifully. The writing is sharp and very funny in ways that sneak up on you. Critics who saw this original production praised exactly that quality, the way Bach uses everyday workplace banter as a kind of camouflage for something much darker underneath. There's a real craft to making an audience laugh while simultaneously unsettling them, and Bach pulls that off. And this play feels genuinely timely right now, perhaps even more so than it would when it premiered. The themes of complicity, of going along with questionable practices because it's just your job, of the casual moral compromises people make within institutions, all of that lands with real weight in this current moment. It is a subversive play in the best sense of the word. So, negatives, I only have one. My one complaint actually is not about the play itself, it's about the pre-show music. And standard note that I always give, the pre-show music is too loud. But beyond the volume, the music just felt wrong for the era of this play. The play seems to be set in the past, and the eclectic pre-show music choices were kind of disconcerting and didn't help set the tone of the play. It's a small thing, but it kind of picked at me. So, was I bored? Not bored at all. 80 minutes, the acting is tremendous, and the writing is sharp and very funny. The whole experience is about slowly uncovering what's really going on with these characters, with this company, and with the relationships between each other. And that keeps you fully engaged from start to finish. I was leaning in the entire time. Was I confused? Well, part of what makes this play work is that it it is deliberately withholding information. You don't get all the answers you might want, and honestly, I think that's a feature, not a bug. After the curtain comes down, you have room to think. You ask yourself, when exactly did Lorraine make the decision she seems to have made? What was the tipping point for each of these characters? The play gives you enough to go on, but leaves you to do some of the work yourself, and I'm fine with that. It's fun to sit with this play. I did have one specific question that lingered with me. The show begins with a monologue from Edward Raymond about catching fish. He explains that if a fish is unharmed, he releases it back into the water. But if it's damaged, say a hook got caught in the gills, he will he will humanely bleed it out in the water so that it slowly loses oxygen, like the fish is going to sleep, and then he eats it. Not not there and then, but later. It's kind of a haunting monologue, and when you understand what Raymond does for work, the juxtaposition is very striking. And I found myself wondering, is this him rationalizing the moral logic of his job, or is this him realizing on some level that he can't keep doing this job? The play doesn't spell it out and honestly, it's fine that it doesn't because this happens at the beginning of the play and then we don't really understand it in the moment and we have to kind of come back to it in our memory to try to piece out what was going on in that monologue, what was going on in his life in that moment when he gives it and who is he giving that monologue to? It seems like the audience, but I don't think it is the audience. So, let me wrap this up. I love this play. It is an 80-minute masterclass in how to do a lot with very little. It's a small cast, a single setting, a premise that seems deceptively simple right up until it isn't. The themes are genuinely important, the execution is smart and funny and unnerving in equal measure and this cast is terrific. The lesson at the heart of this play, that no one walks away unscathed from complicity in something that's wrong, no matter how far down the chain they are, is one worth sitting with, especially right now. So, why should you see this show? If you like great acting, if you like sharp writing, it and theater that trusts you enough to not spell everything out for you, go see the play. It is only 80 minutes, but those 80 minutes are packed and you will be thinking about it on the subway ride home.
